#5157. XRP’s Quantum-Resistant Design Comes Into Focus

Home » Ripple (XRP) » XRP’s Quantum-Resistant Design Comes Into Focus

The foundation behind XRP Ledger aims to mitigate quantum resistance hazards ahead of the practical test.

The chain developers behind Ripple’s native XRP Ledger are actively preparing to implement quantum-resistant measures. For this reason, the devs picked ML-DSA-44, a digital signature standard that the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) approved in 2024.

Earlier this year, Ripple introduced a multi-phase roadmap to prepare the XRP Ledger (XRPL) for a post-quantum future, with a target for full readiness by 2028. The new signature format needs 3,732 bytes for public keys and signatures, raising transaction data requirements. This will be audited in mid 2027.

JUST IN: $XRP Ledger unveils quantum-resistant account plan, allowing users to upgrade to quantum-proof security with no additional transaction fees as Ripple targets full quantum protection by 2028. pic.twitter.com/wS2Mk46nG8

As described in Google’s quantum computing research paper, there’s a few key risks the crypto sphere has to handle. The most quoted one is the exposable public key risks when users transact within the blockchain, something that quantum-computing based hackers could take serious advantage of.

There’s a more subtle risk too, one elliptic curve researchers call “harvest now, decrypt later.” Simply put, bad actors can collect publicly visible cryptographic data from the blockchain today and hold onto it. This raises the chances of the account eventually being broken into.

🚨 MASSIVE: THE $XRP LEDGER IS PREPARING FOR QUANTUM COMPUTERS. HERE IS WHAT NOBODY IS TELLING YOU.Every payment you sign reveals your public key.A powerful enough quantum computer could work backward from it.Any account that has ever sent a payment is already exposed.The… https://t.co/hpCLy5Gzzi pic.twitter.com/L32SemqQcE

The extra XRP network storage needed for this kind of upgrade doesn’t necessarily raise the fees. Node operators are absorbing the ~3.6 KB increase per protected transaction (from 105 bytes to 3,732 bytes for key plus the signature), as documented in the proposal. With database overhead, every secure payment would use 5,331 bytes of storage.

David Schwartz Explains What Could Really Drive XRP's ValueFormer Ripple (@Ripple) CTO David Schwartz (@JoelKatz) says using $XRP to pay XRPL (@XRP) gas fees is unlikely to drive its price significantly.He argues that broader network adoption could create value for XRP… pic.twitter.com/X0et9M7El9

The XRP Ledger foundation is planning the inaugural phase of the quantum resistance study in early 2027 as devs polish the proposition of key generation between the Python, JavaScript and server versions. Mitigations are done within a zero-knowledge proof to validate results without disclosing vectors.

Quantum physics may be a tough nut to crack for most crypto currencies, but XRP’s developers are set on a mission to get the chain shielded by 2028.

#5155. Strategy spent more than twice as much on preferred buybacks as Bitcoin last week

The November 9 filing shows common-stock proceeds funding Bitcoin purchases and a larger STRC buyback during November 2-8.

Bitcoin treasury company Strategy funded its Bitcoin purchases and a larger STRC preferred-stock buyback with common-stock sales during Nov. 2-8, while recording no sales through its four preferred-stock at-the-market programs, according to its Nov. 9 filing.

The company raised $284 million in net proceeds by selling 2,051,348 MSTR common shares. It directed $188 million to STRC repurchases, $82 million to Bitcoin and $14 million to its USD Cash balance.

Common shareholders financed both more Bitcoin and fewer preferred shares outstanding. The repurchases can reduce future preferred-dividend requirements, while issuing MSTR increases the number of common shares. STRC's prospective return as a funding source had yet to produce disclosed sales during that week.

During Nov. 2-8, 2026, common-stock proceeds funded a larger STRC buyback than Bitcoin purchase.

Thanks for signing up to The Catalyst. Look out for your first daily email. If you already receive it, you’re all set.

An improved trading price and a completed capital raise are separate events. In its July 27 policy announcement, Strategy said it would not issue STRC below $100 per share and expected repurchases to taper as the security approached that level. Those policies were statements of intent that could change.

A price recovery can improve the conditions for selling new preferred shares. Cash reaches Strategy when it actually issues them. The latest filing records no STRC sales for Nov. 2-8, nor any sales in the STRF, STRK or STRD ATM rows.

Strategy acquired 1,036 BTC for $82 million during the week, at an average $79,012 per coin including fees and expenses.

The larger use of that capital was the repurchase of 1,887,464 STRC shares for $188 million.

Strategy's issuer briefing explains that common equity sits behind debt and preferred stock, so removing preferred claims can strengthen the residual economics available to common shareholders.

Funding those purchases by issuing common stock increases the share count. Existing holders therefore share the remaining economics with more shares outstanding. Whether the combined transaction improves value per share depends on the issuance terms, repurchase price and use of proceeds.

This extends the capital-allocation tension described in CryptoSlate's Nov. 2 coverage of deployable cash pressure.

As of Nov. 8, Strategy held $4.77 billion in its USD Reserve and $146 million in USD Cash. The reserve is intended to support preferred-stock dividends and interest on outstanding debt. USD Cash serves broader treasury purposes, including buying Bitcoin, expanding the reserve and capital management.

Strategy used $21 million of the reserve to pay preferred dividends during Nov. 2-8. The $14 million allocated from MSTR proceeds went to USD Cash.

@saylor's Nov. 9 post summarized the company's position as 850,364 BTC and about $4.9 billion in USD assets. That broad dollar figure includes balances with distinct designated purposes; the filing separately identifies the cash available for broader treasury deployment.

#5154. Nvidia Board Investigates Jensen Huang After Report He Was Target of Chinese Spy Effort

Nvidia Board Investigates Jensen Huang After Report He Was Target of Chinese Spy Effort

Nvidia's board of directors has opened an independent investigation following reports that CEO Jensen Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort, the company said on Sunday.

A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside counsel, will oversee the inquiry. "While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information," it said, adding that it "has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team."

We just issued a press release from our board of directors. Read the release: https://t.co/W9yXWJzbkk

— NVIDIA Newsroom (@nvidianewsroom) November 8, 2026

The investigation follows a Financial Times report on Saturday that a U.S. government memo, written earlier this year based on intelligence information, said the Nvidia CEO had been romantically involved with Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore-based Nvidia customer Megaspeed, citing people familiar with the memo. U.S. intelligence believes she was recruited by China's Ministry of State Security, the FT reported. Nvidia declined to comment to the newspaper on the memo. Huang's email to staff, sent on Sunday, did not name the person with whom he had an affair.

Lawmakers from both parties are seeking answers. Republican leaders have asked Huang to appear privately before the House China, foreign affairs and intelligence committees, according to the FT, while Sen. Chris Coons (D-DE), who will chair the Senate Foreign Relations Committee from January, pledged in a tweet that "Congress will investigate and get answers."

The FT's report built on a New York Times investigation last month, which said U.S. intelligence agencies had concluded that Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, a Chinese citizen, was a Chinese intelligence asset, and that surveillance of her had revealed a close relationship with Jensen Huang. President Donald Trump was briefed on the findings roughly a year ago and chose not to act on them, according to the Times.

U.S. officials suspected Megaspeed of helping Chinese companies get around restrictions on advanced AI chips, and the Commerce Department's investigation into the company has been handed to the Justice Department, the Times reported. Megaspeed's sister company in Malaysia bought at least $4.8 billion worth of AI equipment containing Nvidia chips between June 2024 and February 2026, according to trade records cited by the newspaper.

Nvidia told the Times that Huang's interactions with Ms. Huang were "not unusual or unexpected," and that customers like Megaspeed receive "ordinary business information." Megaspeed said it had retained outside counsel to conduct an internal investigation, Ms. Huang did not respond to the newspaper's requests for comment, and China's embassy in Washington dismissed the allegations as "groundless smears and slanders."

In an email to employees on Sunday, Huang apologized to his family and colleagues. "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did," he wrote, according to a copy published by CNBC.

"Today's news will not slow NVIDIA. Jensen is committed to continuing to lead NVIDIA as CEO without interruption," the company told CNBC.

Nvidia shares were down 5% at $177.32 in premarket trading early on Monday, after closing at $186.64 on Friday, according to Yahoo Finance.

#5153. Don’t Store Crypto on iPhone, Ledger CTO Says

Ledger Chief Technology Officer Charles Guillemet has recently warned cryptocurrency holders not to store critical wallet information on their iPhones, as the security threat is on the rise.

In his recent post on X, the Ledger executive highlighted the fact that vulnerabilities that can leak important data are now becoming more and more accessible for hackers to exploit.

"Unfortunately this kind of vulnerability used to be very expensive and reserved to high potential attackers," Guillemet tweeted.

However, he pointed out that we're now on the verge of seeing the costs of such vulnerabilities go down to zero, meaning that it could become very easy for cybercriminals to exploit them on a massive scale.

"Simply don't store any valuable in your mobile. Especially not your crypto seeds," the Ledger CTO cautioned.

His words came in response to an urgent security alert published by crypto exchange Binance over a vulnerability that was found in Apple's iOS operating system.

In particular, cryptocurrency exchange Binance reported a vulnerability, dubbed worse_query, which can allow malicious applications to gain access to files of other applications installed on the same device.

As specified by the exchange, this security flaw affects iOS 26.7.1, 27.0.1 and 27.2.

This means that crypto wallet recovery phrases, private keys and login credentials can be at risk, as they may be stored in accessible local files.

Binance underscored that this concern isn't exclusive to the exchange's app alone, while adding that the vulnerability can have an impact on the entire crypto space.

The exchange recommended that users uninstall apps that were downloaded from untrusted sources, update their operating systems and avoid installing any unauthorized software.

Binance also advised users to transfer their funds to newly created wallets on clean devices if they think their wallets may have been compromised.

Apple published new security updates on Nov. 9. However, it's not clear if they are enough to fully patch this vulnerability. Still, there have been no confirmed crypto thefts specifically linked to the exploit.

Guillemet's warning comes a month after Ledger's major security incident involving compromised hardware wallets.

Back in October, French cryptocurrency hardware wallet maker Ledger admitted that some hardware wallets distributed by its Southeast Asian reseller CryptoBilis had been tampered with.

It turned out that hackers managed to install complex hardware implants in legitimate Ledger devices. With that, hackers were able to intercept users' recovery phrases when people were setting up their Ledger wallets for the first time.

As shown by Ledger's investigation, malicious implants were capable of capturing the 24-word recovery phrase that appears on the Ledger device screen and then passing it to attackers via a cellular connection.

Blockchain sleuths estimated that this incident might have led to more than $86 million in crypto losses. However, Ledger itself didn't confirm the total amount.

#5151. Top 12 Crypto Debit Cards to Consider

Home » Cryptopedia » Top 12 Crypto Debit Cards to Consider

Compare fees, cashback, availability, and features of 12 crypto cards to find the right option for your spending needs.

Crypto debit cards are no longer just a way to convert Bitcoin into cash for everyday purchases. In 2026, there are plenty of options, from exchange-linked cards and stablecoin payment solutions to self-custody cards connected directly to crypto wallets.

But choosing one isn’t just about cashback. Availability depends on your country, better rewards may require staking or a paid subscription, and fees can quickly eat into your benefits. It’s also worth checking how each card works, as some are prepaid debit cards while others offer credit backed by crypto holdings.

We’ve selected 12 crypto cards worth considering in 2026, comparing their features, fees, rewards, and availability to help you find the right option, whether you prioritize low fees, stablecoin spending, cashback, or control over your assets.

The Coinbase Card Visa prepaid debit card that lets US customers (excluding Hawaii) spend directly from their Coinbase accounts.

It is a custodial card, meaning funds remain in your Coinbase account and are deducted when you make a purchase. Coinbase automatically converts crypto to USD at checkout or for ATM withdrawals, so merchants never receive crypto. You also get a virtual card as soon as you’re approved, with Apple Pay and Google Pay support.

Fees are relatively low. There are no annual fees or charges for spending USD or crypto, including USDC. Coinbase Card does not charge monthly or foreign transaction fees, and there are no Coinbase ATM withdrawal fees (though ATM operators may charge their own). The main cost is Coinbase’s crypto conversion spread. Spending USD or USDC avoids it, making them the cheapest funding options.

Crypto rewards are the main attraction, but rates vary. Rewards are optional, available to US users, and paid in a crypto asset of your choice from a rotating list. Rates are displayed in the app, can be changed at any time, and have no stated cap. Although many reviews advertise rates of up to 4%, Coinbase does not guarantee a fixed rate on its official card page. Check the current in-app offer before applying.

Best for: US-based Coinbase users who want a simple, low-fee card and crypto rewards without a credit check.

Crypto.com’s crypto debit card depends on your region. In the US, it is now a Visa Signature credit card issued by Comenity Capital Bank through Bread Financial. Cardholders can earn rewards in BTC or CRO, but approval requires a credit check. Applications are made through the Crypto.com app.

Rewards range from roughly 1.5% to 5–6%, depending on the tier. However, higher Level Up tiers require locking up or staking CRO. Those who don’t want to commit CRO can choose the entry tier.

Outside the US, the card remains a prepaid debit card. In the European Economic Area (EEA), the free tier offers no cashback, while the Plus plan (€4.99/month) starts at 2% cashback.

Best for: Users who already hold CRO and want to maximize rewards.

KAST is a Visa debit card that that spends a USD balance funded with stablecoins. It offers three tiers: Standard (free, 1.5% cashback), Premium ($1000 a year, 2% cashback) and Private ($10,000 a year, 3%).

Cashback is paid in dollars, rather than tokens. Monthly cashback limits apply: $2,000 in spend for Standard, $10,000 for Premium and $40,000 for Private.

However, KAST fees can reduce the returns. Foreign exchange fees on KAS crypto debit card range from 0.5% to 1.75%, while a physical Standard card costs $40 to deliver.

KAST estimates Standard users may keep up to 1% cashback after FX fees. Premium and Private also include a Visa Infinite card and KAST Points on eligible spending.

Best for: Fequent stablecoin spenders, especially those spending in USD.

Krak, Kraken’s money app, launched its Visa debit card in the US in August 2026. Available as a physical and virtual card, it lets users spend from 600+ fiat and crypto assets, with purchases converted to USD at checkout. The card is issued by Lead Bank and powered by Stripe Issuing.

Krak offers up to 2% cashback in USD or Bitcoin, paid after transactions settle, with no monthly or annual fees.

Rewards depend on users’ average asset balances across Krak, Kraken and Kraken Pro. The card is available in all US states except New York, Maine, Massachusetts and Indiana. Crypto-funded purchases may incur conversion spreads and trigger taxable events.

Best for: US users who hold a mix of crypto and cash and want one card for everything.

The MetaMask Card lets users spend directly from their self-custody wallet, without preloading funds. Built with Mastercard and Baanx (now Monavate) and issued by Cross River Bank in the US, it works wherever Mastercard is accepted, including online, in-store and through Apple Pay or Google Pay. Unlike exchange cards, MetaMask Card allows to retain full control of your crypto until purchase.

The card has two tiers: the standard card offers 1% cashback in mUSD, while the Metal card costs $199/year and offers 3% cashback on up to $10,000 in annual spending, no foreign transaction fees and higher limits.

Outside the US, it is available in Argentina, Brazil, Canada, Colombia, the EEA, Mexico, Switzerland and the UK. The trade-off is that users take full responsibility for securing their own assets.

Best for: Existing MetaMask users who want to keep control of their keys.

The Nexo Card is a Mastercard issued by DiPocket UAB, a Lithuanian-licensed e-money institution (EMI). It offers two app-controlled modes: Credit Mode, which lets users borrow against their crypto without selling it, and Debit Mode.

Cashback depends on Nexo’s loyalty tier, portfolio balance, and card mode. Rewards are paid in NEXO tokens or BTC, with payouts changeable at any time. Rates can reach 2% in NEXO or 0.5% in BTC, although Nexo’s regional page lists up to 2% cashback for credit card holders.

The card is available to eligible users in selected European markets, including the EEA and UK.

Best for: European long-term holders who want liquidity without selling.

The Bybit Card is a Mastercard debit card linked to your Bybit account. In the EEA and Switzerland, it is issued by Moorwand Ltd and Harmoniie SAS, with a 0.5% FX fee on top of Mastercard’s rate and a 0.9% crypto conversion fee.

Availability is limited to selected markets, including the EEA, Switzerland, Australia, Argentina, Brazil, parts of Asia Pacific, and Mexico.

Rewards depend on spending tiers or VIP status, not a flat cashback rate. The advertised “up to 10%” applies only to top tiers.

Fees and limits vary by region, and cashback without VIP status can be minimal, particularly outside Europe. US users should consider alternatives.

Best for: Non-US Bybit traders who want to spend without leaving the crypto exchange.

RedotPay is a custodial Visa card for global stablecoin users, allowing crypto spending in over 100 countries.

It costs $10 for a virtual card or $100 for a physical one, with no monthly or annual fees, and supports major assets including USDT, USDC, BTC, ETH, BNB and SOL.

Standard pricing includes a 1% crypto-to-fiat conversion fee for USD transactions and an additional 1.2% FX markup.

Standard RedotPay accounts offer no ongoing cashback, relying on welcome bonuses and referral rewards. However, its optional RedotPay Pro membership offers 3% cashback on eligible Apple Pay and Google Pay purchases.

The card is unavailable in the US, Canada, China, Japan, South Korea, the Philippines and Russia.

Best for: Freelancers and remote workers paid in USDT outside the US.

Uphold relaunched its US debit card in October 2025, advertising up to 6% in XRP rewards, with additional benefits for direct deposit users. Actual rates vary by tier and conditions, with some sources citing up to 4%. The US offers Essential and Elite plans, both paying rewards exclusively in XRP.

Essential has no annual fee but charges $4.99 for a physical card, $2.95 per ATM withdrawal, and $1.50 in foreign transaction fees.

Elite costs $99.99 annually, includes a metal card, and waives Uphold ATM and foreign transaction fees.

Crypto-funded spending may involve spreads and taxable events. Availability varies by state, while UK users receive a separate program offering 1% cashback in GBP.

Best for: US users who want a multi-asset card and are comfortable earning XRP.

Ether.fi Cash is a non-custodial Visa card that connects DeFi assets to everyday spending. Users can pay directly with USDC or LiquidUSD, or borrow against their crypto without selling it.

The card combines debit-style direct payments with crypto-backed credit. Rewards reach 3% in USDC for most users and 4% for VIP members on the first $50,000.

It offers up to 3% cashback in USDC for most users, rising to 4% for VIP members on the first $50,000 spent. Fees and eligibility vary by tier and region, with some benefits requiring ETHFI staking.

Best for: experienced DeFi users already inside the ether.fi ecosystem.

The Bitpanda Card is a simple Visa debit card for EEA residents. It is available in all Eurozone countries except Cyprus, and requires a verified Bitpanda account and the mobile app.

The card offers 1% cashback on eligible crypto spending, access to more than 600 crypto assets, no monthly fee and no FX fees charged by Bitpanda, although Visa mark-ups may apply.

There are a few important exclusions: stablecoins, precious metals, Bitpanda Stocks and fiat balances do not qualify for cashback. Each payment also triggers a trade, meaning standard trading fees apply. ATM withdrawals cost 2%, with a minimum fee of €2.

Best for: Euro-area users who already invest with Bitpanda.

Gate Card is a custodial crypto debit card linked to your Gate account, available in virtual and physical Visa or Mastercard versions, depending on region. Compatible cards support Apple Pay and Google Pay, with instant virtual issuance.

Cashback ranges from 1% to 8%, depending on your VIP tier or monthly spending. Rewards are issued as points redeemable for USDT, GT and other supported assets, subject to monthly limits of $5–$400.

Fees vary by card, but the latest Blue and AI versions offer free issuance and no monthly fee, with a 0.9% top-up fee and 1.5–1.7% FX fee. Their limits reach $150,000 daily and $1 million monthly.

Level 2 KYC is required. The international service excludes certain jurisdictions, including the US, where a separate Gate US Visa card is available under different terms.

Best for: Existing Gate users who want crypto spending with tier-based rewards and are comfortable keeping funds on a custodial exchange.

The best crypto debit card depends on how you plan to use it, where you live, and which features matter most. Before applying, consider these five factors:

Not every crypto card works worldwide. Some are restricted to the US, EEA, UK, or selected countries. Check whether the provider supports residents of your country and whether the card offers the same features in your region.

Look beyond monthly and annual fees. Crypto conversion spreads, foreign exchange markups, ATM withdrawal charges, and card issuance costs can all affect how much you actually spend.

Compare the rewards you can realistically earn, not just the highest advertised percentage. Some providers require staking, paid subscriptions, or minimum spending levels to unlock better rates. Also check whether rewards are paid in cash, stablecoins, or volatile crypto assets.

Exchange-linked cards generally rely on custodial accounts, while self-custody products can allow users to retain control of their assets until payment. Understand who controls your funds and what happens if your account or wallet is compromised.

Some crypto cards offer prepaid spending, while others provide credit backed by crypto collateral. These products have different risks, repayment requirements, and potential tax implications. Make sure you understand which type you are applying for.

Traditional debit cards use money held in a bank account, while crypto debit cards are linked to cryptocurrency exchanges, digital wallets or stablecoin balances.

When making a payment, some crypto cards automatically convert your digital assets into fiat currency. Others let you spend stablecoins directly or borrow against your crypto holdings.

The main differences come down to funding, custody, fees and rewards. Crypto cards can offer cashback in digital assets and easier access to crypto funds, but may also involve conversion fees, additional account requirements and tax implications.

In some jurisdictions, spending crypto is treated as a taxable disposal. It’s worth checking the local tax rules before using crypto for everyday payments.

Crypto debit cards make it easier to use digital assets for everyday purchases, whether through crypto-funded payments, stablecoin spending or cashback rewards.

But the benefits aren’t always as good as they look. Conversion spreads, foreign transaction fees, subscription costs and staking requirements can eat into your rewards.

The best card depends on how you plan to use it. If low fees matter most, an exchange-linked card may be enough. If you prefer greater control over your assets or want to spend stablecoins, other options may be more suitable. For cashback, look beyond the advertised rate and factor in all associated costs.

Ultimately, choose a card that fits your spending habits, location and risk tolerance. Check the latest fees and terms, and don’t overlook potential tax implications.

A crypto debit card is a payment card linked to a cryptocurrency exchange account or digital wallet. It allows users to make purchases at merchants that accept its payment network, with crypto or stablecoins converted into fiat currency when required.

No. Availability depends on the card issuer, payment provider, and local regulations. Some cards are restricted to US residents, while others support selected European, Asian, or Latin American markets. Features and fees may also differ between regions.

Some crypto debit cards have no annual or monthly fees, but other costs may apply. These include crypto conversion spreads, foreign exchange fees, ATM withdrawal charges, issuance fees, and paid membership subscriptions.

It depends on the card. Many custodial cards convert cryptocurrency into fiat currency when a payment is processed. Some self-custody cards allow users to retain control of their assets until the transaction takes place, while crypto-backed credit products may allow spending without an immediate sale.

Tax treatment depends on your country and the type of reward. Spending appreciated cryptocurrency may trigger a taxable disposal, while cashback and promotional rewards can have different tax treatment. Consult the applicable tax rules in your jurisdiction.

#5150. Slower US inflation leaves Waller’s half-point December hike in play

Core CPI rose 0.3% for a third consecutive month, matching the level Waller linked to considering a half-point December hike before the release.

US monthly headline inflation slowed in October, but core prices rose 0.3% for a third consecutive month, matching the level Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller had associated with considering a 50-basis-point December interest-rate hike.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported on Nov. 10 that consumer prices increased 0.4% from September, seasonally adjusted, after September's 0.6% rise. Core CPI, which excludes food and energy, rose 0.3%. The agency did not publish headline or core year-over-year rates.

That leaves a policy tension beneath the slower headline figure. In prepared remarks earlier that day, before the release, Waller said core CPI around 0.3% or higher would warrant considering a 50-basis-point December hike if the report resembled the preceding two monthly readings. He had leaned toward 25 basis points under his expected outlook.

October's core reading matches that approximate level. The comparison does not establish Waller's assessment after the release or a decision by the Federal Open Market Committee.

Prices continued to increase in October, even though the overall monthly pace eased. Energy rose 0.7%, following a much larger 5.2% increase in September. Food prices also increased, with the index rising 0.5% in October.

Shelter increased 0.3% and accounted for more than 30% of the monthly headline increase, according to BLS.

The core result shows why the headline slowdown offers only part of the picture. Removing food and energy leaves the same 0.3% monthly increase recorded in August and September. There was no corresponding improvement in that monthly measure.

October's unchanged monthly core reading matches the approximate level Waller cited before the release when discussing December.

Slower headline inflation coexists with the core reading Waller had linked to considering 50 basis points.

Monthly changes, not annual inflation. Waller's conditional personal remarks preceded the release; neither a post-release endorsement nor an FOMC decision is established. Most October annual comparisons, including headline and core, are unavailable.

Slope chart plots reported September and October seasonally adjusted monthly CPI rates on one linear 0%-0.6% scale. Dashed connector marks an editorial comparison with Waller's approximate core CPI condition, not causation or a policy trigger. Basis points describe the possible rate move, not CPI.

Price changes also varied across categories. Recreation rose 0.8% and motor vehicle insurance increased 0.7%, while used cars and trucks fell 1.2%. Those differences matter when assessing a report that combines slower overall inflation with continuing pressure in several components.

Waller's remarks explicitly state that the views are his own and do not necessarily represent colleagues on the Fed Board or the FOMC.

Waller separately discussed personal consumption expenditures inflation, the measure targeted by the FOMC. The comparison with October's release concerns core CPI; the two measures should not be treated as interchangeable.

BLS did not publish October year-over-year changes for headline or core CPI. During the 2025 lapse in appropriations, the agency did not collect October 2025 survey data, leaving most series without the prior-year indexes needed for an annual calculation.

For Bitcoin readers, the immediate policy question is how officials assess persistent core inflation alongside the slower headline pace.

The next test is policymakers' post-release assessment and subsequent inflation evidence ahead of December. BLS has scheduled November's CPI report for Dec. 10 at 8:30 a.m. Eastern.

The Head of Ripple Prime, Marc Asch, is stepping down from the company by the end of 2015, according to a CoinDesk report citing a Ripple spokesperson.

#5148. Bittensor gains 3% after Tencent’s AI launch – Can subnet fees lift TAO?

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Is Q4 shaping up to be the most bullish quarter yet for decentralized AI?

The whole of the AI market has come under increased scrutiny recently. The release of earnings from big tech companies such as Amazon shows just how expensive expanding into AI can be. Their stock dropped nearly 8% in a short span of time, causing over $200 billion to be wiped off their value.

While the stock has since recovered most of its losses, gaining over 11% so far in November, the sell-off was still a major reality check for investors.

This raises an important question: Could growing concerns over Big Tech’s AI spending become a catalyst for decentralized AI networks?

Recently, Bittensor has seen an uptick in momentum as one of its subnets (Chutes) was chosen by Tencent as a launch partner for their new flagship AI model HY4.

The key takeaway? Tencent has a combined 1.439 billion monthly active users on their Weixin and WeChat platforms.

Chutes charges $0.525 per million input tokens and $1.5625 per million output tokens. This shows how decentralized AI providers are competing on cost while reaching larger markets.

Notably, the impact is also reflected in the market.

Bittensor’s [TAO] price has risen by more than 3% to trade at $220. This comes after the partnership with Tencent, amid increasing worries about the increasing costs of AI in Big Tech. This raises an important question: Could AI be emerging as a key driver of crypto’s growing divergence from the broader market?

Strategically, Bittensor is positioning itself at the center of the growing AI trend.

The affordable services it offers are becoming more attractive, especially with the new partnership with Tencent that gives access to a whole ecosystem with close to 1.5 billion monthly active users.

This can increase Bittensor’s exposure, allowing for more decentralised AI adoption. So, to track how this trend could impact the wider AI crypto sector, TAO will be a key token to watch.

Interestingly, this momentum is also starting to show up on-chain. The Bittensor-based decentralized AI platform Almanac (SN41) generated $109,440 in fees during October. This is the first time it has exceeded $100k in fees.

The interesting part? Almanac burned 100% of these fees to buy back TAO and SN41 alpha.

Meanwhile, Engy (SN53), a Bittensor subnet dedicated to providing verifiable AI inference for open-source models, has already spent $63,000 on buybacks and token burns.

Together, these developments highlight how growing subnet revenue is translating into direct buying pressure for TAO.

However, the key test will be whether this momentum can translate into real market demand. TAO’s recent 3% rally suggests that investor interest may already be picking up.

So, if more subnets continue generating revenue and using it for token buybacks and burns, Bittensor could build a stronger fundamental case and become one of the strongest plays in the decentralised AI sector heading into 2027.

Tencent’s partnership with Chutes puts Bittensor in front of nearly 1.5 billion users, boosting its exposure to the AI market.

Growing subnet revenue and token buybacks are supporting TAO demand, while its 3% rally signals rising interest in decentralized AI.

#5147. Trump Says He Knows 'Nothing' About World Liberty Financial as He Defends UAE Ties

Trump Says He Knows 'Nothing' About World Liberty Financial as He Defends UAE Ties

U.S. President Donald Trump has defended his family's stake in crypto venture World Liberty Financial, saying he knows "nothing" about the firm despite being a co-owner, in an interview after last week's midterm elections.

Asked by columnist Ross Douthat why his co-ownership of a company partly owned by investors linked to the United Arab Emirates government was different from the kind of arrangement he would call corrupt if it involved the Biden family, Trump replied: "Here's the difference [... ] I'm gonna tell you why. Because I know nothing about it," according to a transcript published by CBS News.

Pressed on why he did not simply divest, Trump said most of his money is managed by Wall Street firms through index funds, and that his sons run the family business. "It's hard to say to them, 'Don't do anything anymore for four years because I'm president,'" he said.

When Douthat asked whether foreign investors in the company believe they are buying influence, Trump said: "I don't know." He argued that conflicts of interest have dogged presidents "going back to George Washington," adding that past presidents "own something, whatever crypto was at the time."

"There's crypto, and before that there was oil," Trump said, adding that, "every president has had this problem."

"I'm a bigger name than other presidents, whether we like it or not," Trump said.

World Liberty Financial, which Eric Trump announced in August 2024, issues the WLFI governance token and the USD1 stablecoin. In January, it launched World Liberty Markets, a lending and borrowing platform built on DeFi protocol Dolomite.

Its UAE links have drawn scrutiny from Democrats. Aryam Investment, a UAE-backed entity tied to the country's national security adviser, Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed, agreed to buy a 49% stake in World Liberty Financial for $500 million four days before Trump's January 2025 inauguration, Decrypt reported in February, citing The Wall Street Journal. The deal, signed by Eric Trump on World Liberty's behalf, reportedly preceded the administration's reversal of restrictions on advanced AI chip sales to the UAE. A World Liberty spokesperson said at the time that neither Trump nor his Middle East envoy, Steve Witkoff, had "any involvement whatsoever" in the transaction, ABC News reported. Sen. Chris Murphy (D-CT) described the arrangement in February as "potentially criminal conduct." Trump has previously said he was not aware of the deal.

The company's UAE ties have also surfaced in its legal battle with Tron founder Justin Sun. Sun's lawyers asked a federal court to sanction World Liberty, alleging the firm delayed disclosing UAE ownership that could defeat federal jurisdiction over his lawsuit. World Liberty has called Sun's legal campaign a "meritless PR stunt."

The Trump family's financial stake in the venture is set out in World Liberty's own disclosures. DT Marks DEFI LLC, an entity affiliated with Trump and certain family members, owns about 38% of the holding company behind World Liberty Financial, holds 22.5 billion WLFI tokens, and is entitled to 75% of the net proceeds from WLFI token sales, according to the company. A separate Trump-affiliated entity has an indirect claim on interest earned on the reserves backing USD1. The disclosures state that no member of the Trump family is an officer, director or employee of World Liberty, though Trump's sons have remained involved with the company, Decrypt reported earlier this year.

#5143. AI-assisted firms increase flaw disclosures by 120% with no detected repair slowdown, study finds

A preprint found a roughly 120% relative increase in disclosures against a Chinese-firm comparison group, with no detectable slowdown in the repair channels studied.

Software-flaw disclosures at firms given early access to Anthropic's AI model Claude Mythos Preview rose by roughly 120% relative to the change at Chinese firms without access, a November 4 preprint finds. Measured repair times showed no detectable slowdown.

Thomas Mosk's study finds that AI-assisted bug hunting was associated with more public disclosures without a detectable slowdown in the repair channels studied. Its findings cover publicly disclosed vulnerabilities and specific repair channels, leaving undisclosed workloads and users' installation of patches unmeasured.

Anthropic announced Project Glasswing on April 7, giving selected firms access to the model. The main disclosure analysis compares 13 participants with 267 Chinese firms from October 2025 through September 2026. The Chinese firms could use other AI tools. Selection into Glasswing was not random, and national disclosure practices differ, limiting causal interpretation.

Alongside the 120% relative increase in disclosures, the paper estimates roughly 150% more high-impact disclosures. That category means an above-median impact component in the vulnerability severity score.

Earlier Epoch AI analysis, published July 2, documented a spike in high- and critical-severity disclosures after Mythos Preview. It also warned that public counts omit undisclosed discoveries and can reflect increased interest in bug hunting.

Mosk examines fixing capacity separately, comparing Glasswing vulnerabilities with other non-Chinese vulnerabilities in shorter samples. One analysis follows 658 flaws reported to vendors by the Zero Day Initiative through June 2026. Another covers 14,855 vulnerabilities published through July and tracked by Linux distributions including Debian, Ubuntu, Red Hat and SUSE.

Neither repair channel showed a statistically detectable slowdown. For disclosed flaws, the distributions' median time to a fix stayed at one day. The vendor estimates rule out a slowdown larger than about 13%, although smaller changes remain possible. The downstream estimates still permit an approximately 11 percentage-point decline in the share fixed within 90 days.

For crypto infrastructure, the practical distinction is between finding a flaw, releasing a fix and installing it. CryptoSlate reported on Oct. 29 that Bitcoin Core disclosed three AI-discovered flaws after validation and patch releases. Installation across nodes remains a separate question.

The exploitation results also require care. In a comparison with large non-Chinese firms ending in May, before Glasswing's June expansion, Mosk found no statistically significant change in exploited-vulnerability counts across one-, two- and three-month windows.

The share of disclosed flaws known to be exploited fell in some comparisons. A larger pool of disclosures can lower that share without reducing exploited-vulnerability counts, however. Mosk treats the probability decline as suggestive; the count estimates remain too imprecise to exclude moderate changes in either direction.

#5141. Coinbase Joins Circle, Ripple With Final OCC Approval for Federal Trust Bank Charter

Coinbase Joins Circle, Ripple With Final OCC Approval for Federal Trust Bank Charter

Coinbase has received final approval from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) to charter Coinbase National Trust Company, the crypto exchange said on Monday.

The OCC approved the application last Friday, according to Coinbase. The firm said the charter will let it expand its custody business, which holds digital assets on behalf of institutional clients, under a federal regulatory framework.

"Custody is foundational to our business," the company said, describing itself as the leading crypto custodian globally. The charter will "bring clear and consistent federal uniformity" to its custody operations, it added.

"Trusted custody is essential for bringing more of the financial system onchain," Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong tweeted on Monday, calling the trust company "another step for building that foundation."

Trusted custody is essential for bringing more of the financial system onchain.

Coinbase National Trust Company is another step for building that foundation. https://t.co/35K2yC3xpj

— Brian Armstrong (@brian_armstrong) November 9, 2026

Coinbase has offered regulated custody since 2018, when its Coinbase Custody Trust Company won a limited purpose trust charter from the New York Department of Financial Services. The new national trust company builds on that foundation while bringing its trust activities into a consistent federal framework, Coinbase said.

The approval comes seven months after the OCC gave Coinbase conditional approval in April, when the company said it was not becoming a commercial bank and would not take retail deposits or engage in fractional reserve banking. Coinbase first applied for the charter last year.

Coinbase joins a growing list of crypto firms with national trust charters. Circle won final approval in July for a trust bank to manage the reserves behind its USDC stablecoin, and Ripple received final approval last month for a trust bank behind its RLUSD stablecoin.

Others are still awaiting final approval. Jack Dorsey's Block has applied for a charter to custody Bitcoin in September, Kraken parent Payward filed its own application in May, and a trust company linked to Trump family-backed World Liberty Financial won conditional approval in August for a charter tied to its USD1 stablecoin, Reuters reported.

The approvals have drawn opposition. Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-MA) has argued that the OCC's crypto charter approvals, including Coinbase's, are illegal, and the Independent Community Bankers of America has sued the OCC in an effort to stop crypto firms from entering banking through what it describes as a side door.

#5140. Bitcoin’s projected difficulty cut would still leave older S19 rigs short at 5-cent power

At unchanged Bitcoin price, subsidy and fees, the projected 6.5% difficulty cut would leave modeled 95 and 90 TH/s S19s below electricity coverage at 5 cents/kWh.

Bitcoin miners could earn about 7% more per unit of computing power if a projected difficulty cut materializes, but the relief would leave two older S19 variants needing electricity near 4 cents per kilowatt-hour just to cover machine power.

Hashrate Index’s November 9 snapshot, dated 18:00 UTC, projected a 6.5% difficulty reduction around November 13. The mining data platform put current difficulty at 148.36 trillion and spot hashprice at $31.89 per petahash per second per day. Hashprice measures expected daily revenue from a unit of mining capacity, before expenses.

With Bitcoin’s price, block subsidy and average transaction fees per block unchanged, that projected cut would lift hashprice to about $34.11. It would improve the electricity cushion for miners still operating, while leaving a large gap between older equipment and a more efficient S21.

Lower difficulty increases the probability that a given amount of computing work earns a block reward. Expected revenue per unit of work therefore moves inversely with difficulty when the value of rewards stays fixed.

The scenario calculation divides $31.89 by 0.935, the share of difficulty remaining after a 6.5% reduction. That produces a 7% increase and isolates the retarget’s effect. Actual dollar receipts would also depend on Bitcoin pricing and fees.

Bitcoin recalculates difficulty every 2,016 blocks, using block timestamps to target roughly two weeks. November 13 and the size of the cut remain estimates that can change as more blocks arrive.

The useful operating test is the highest electricity tariff gross mining revenue can cover. Dividing expected daily receipts by the machine’s daily wall-power consumption gives that electricity-only ceiling. A tariff below the ceiling leaves something toward other expenses; a tariff above it means machine electricity alone exceeds gross revenue.

BITMAIN’s S19 specifications list two model 240-Ca variants at 95 and 90 terahashes per second, both drawing a nominal 3,250 watts at 25 degrees Celsius. Its S21 specification lists 200 TH/s at 3,500 watts under the same temperature condition.

The calculations assume continuous operation at nominal ratings and a 6.5% difficulty cut, with Bitcoin price, subsidy and average fees per block unchanged. They exclude pool fees, separate cooling and site loads, repairs, labor, hosting overhead, financing and equipment costs.

#5138. Microsoft-Backed Space and Time Launches Platform to Let AI Agents Verify Private Data

Microsoft-Backed Space and Time Launches Platform to Let AI Agents Verify Private Data

Space and Time, a Microsoft-backed blockchain data project, has launched a platform designed to let businesses use private data in AI tools without handing over the underlying records, the company announced on Monday.

Space and Time Enterprise lets companies prove that calculations made on their private data are correct, so that AI applications, auditors and other stakeholders can check the results without accessing the database itself. Launch partners include onchain asset manager Maple Finance, Indonesian vehicle maker and distributor Indomobil, Oracle software consultancy Trenez and AI data network The Data Foundation.

"Businesses want AI agents to execute workflows using that information, but those agents don't need unrestricted access to the records behind every calculation," Nate Holiday, CEO of MakeInfinite Labs, the original developer of Space and Time, told Decrypt.

The stakes are high, he argued. "The potential cost to a business is the overall value of the business," Holiday said. "Giving AI tools unrestricted access to data creates another avenue of exposure."

Holiday said the company is working with customers in industries including construction, engineering and manufacturing that want to rebuild their systems around AI, so that agents, reporting tools and compliance teams can work from the same business records and check the calculations they rely on.

The platform is built on Proof of SQL, Space and Time's patented technology for proving that database queries were computed correctly. It already works with Google Cloud's BigQuery, and businesses can now run it on their own servers without operating a blockchain, buying specialized hardware or relying on an outside proving service, according to the company.

With GPU acceleration, supported queries over millions of rows can be run and proven in under a second, Holiday said, though actual performance depends on the query, hardware and dataset.

The technology proves that a calculation was carried out correctly on a given set of records, but it cannot tell whether those records were accurate to begin with. "An incorrect entry still needs to be caught through the business's data controls," Holiday said, "but verification gives those controls a much stronger foundation: evidence of which data was used and whether it was processed correctly."

Space and Time raised $20 million in 2022 in a strategic funding round led by M12, Microsoft's venture fund. Last year, Grayscale launched a trust giving investors exposure to SXT, the token that powers Space and Time's blockchain. Earlier this year, the company launched Dreamspace, an AI-powered tool built with Microsoft's Azure AI services that lets users create and deploy onchain apps without writing code.

Space and Time also runs SXT Chain, a decentralized network that supplies verifiable data to DeFi, tokenized assets and stablecoins. #5136. Onramp Launches Business Bitcoin Accounts With Two-Person Withdrawal Approvals as Wrench Attacks Climb

Onramp launched Onramp Business on Tuesday, a free company account with named users, role-based permissions and two-person withdrawal approvals, as physical attacks on bitcoin holders climbed in the first half of the year.

The Austin firm announced the product for companies that want bitcoin on the balance sheet but have balked at leaving it with a single login, a single custodian or a single keyholder. The base account carries a 0.85% trade fee, holds bitcoin at a qualified custodian and is usually verified within a business day. It supports up to three users, including owner, admin and view-only roles, plus an audit trail. Two higher tiers, Onramp Treasury and Onramp Enterprise, launched alongside it.

“We spent years watching businesses decide they wanted bitcoin on the balance sheet, then stall the moment their board asked who holds the keys,” said Michael Tanguma, founder and CEO of Onramp. “Nobody had a good answer. Onramp Business gives a company the same controls its bank account already has: named users, approvals on withdrawals, and a record of everything. As the position grows, Onramp Treasury holds it in a vault protected by three independent institutions, so no single party, Onramp included, can lose or move it.”

A midyear report recorded 52 physical attacks on bitcoin and crypto holders in the first half of 2026, up 33% from a year earlier. Recorded exposure tied to those incidents rose to about $124 million from $10.5 million. The report notes that a person who can move coins alone can be forced to do so under duress.

Onramp Business itself is not Multi-Institution Custody. Bitcoin in the free account sits in cold storage at a qualified custodian, the company’s product page says. Multi-Institution Custody comes with Onramp Treasury, which starts at $375 a month, or $3,600 a year, cuts the trade fee to 0.65% and moves the coins into a vault held in the company’s name.

That vault is protected by a 2-of-3 quorum of Onramp, Tetra Trust and CoinCover, so no single institution can lose, move or use the bitcoin. Treasury supports up to five users and two vaults, and includes migration help and continuity planning for leadership changes. A $500 onboarding fee is waived for companies that activate Treasury by Dec. 31. Onramp Enterprise, aimed at funds, miners and large corporate treasuries, is priced by consultation.

Onramp has offered Multi-Institution Custody for individuals and institutions since 2023, with a network that also includes BitGo. The firm raised $12.5 million in a Series A in May at a $135 million valuation and has said it holds more than $1 billion in bitcoin under the model, with no security incidents since it was founded. It also launched Onramp Finance in April, combining cash, bitcoin brokerage, IRAs and gold.

Public companies have turned bitcoin into a balance-sheet asset at a scale that would have been unusual a few years ago. Strategy (MSTR), the largest corporate holder, now holds 850,364 bitcoin after its latest weekly purchase. For smaller firms, the harder question has often been operational: who holds the keys, what happens when that person leaves, and whether a single compromised login or a single coerced employee can move the whole position.

Pacific Office Designs and Build Collateral Agent are already using Onramp for company bitcoin, the announcement said.

“As collateral agent for credit funds using bitcoin as collateral, Build Collateral Agent, LLC selects partners based on a number of risk mitigation considerations, including our attempt to eliminate single points of failure,” said John Ruth, president of Build Collateral Agent, LLC. “Onramp Business uses a differentiated approach with their multi-institutional security model that is aligned with our risk mitigation philosophy. Onramp’s service model has exceeded our expectations. Team members and leadership are available to us when we need them – providing valuable human connections to a tech savvy product suite.”

The test now is whether boards that liked the asset but rejected the custody options will treat two-person approvals, and a three-institution vault, as enough of an answer.

#5135. DeepMind says its AI agents ran a four-day cryptography test with about 20 human messages

The agents coded, ran and debugged a known RSA benchmark over nearly four days, with human approval gates and a large computing budget.

Google DeepMind says two AI agents reproduced a known 1024-bit cryptography computation over nearly four days with about 20 human messages, mostly approvals, carrying the research through coding, large-scale execution and debugging.

The test concerns RSA digital signatures. After billions of advance queries to a simulated signing service, the agents computed a mathematical root needed for a new signature once access ended. They did not recover a private key.

The working paper reports 391 CPU core-years for the completed computation, compared with an earlier team's rounded 1,380 on the same instance and algorithm. That is about a 3.5-fold reduction in measured CPU use. GPU work and preliminary probes are excluded.

DeepMind researcher @pushmeet announced the work on Nov. 6, describing a sandboxed reproduction of a previously solved benchmark instance. The papers say these results do not threaten deployed cryptosystems based on 2048-bit or larger RSA.

The human chose the problem, instance and limits on the signing service, then approved conditions for irreversible steps. According to the paper, the researcher wrote no code, launched no jobs and diagnosed no faults.

A supervisor agent maintained the design, budgets and checks. An executor wrote and tested code, launched distributed jobs and repaired failures. The supervisor also enlisted a specialist sub-agent to accelerate one linear-algebra step.

The agents produced about 33,500 new lines of code, ran 336 distributed experiments and exchanged 218 messages. From design to the verified result, the work took three days and 22 hours.

Their first computed root was wrong because a 32-bit offset overflowed. A correctness check caught the error, and the agents located and fixed it without repeating the advance signing queries. Limited human messaging still came with a human-selected task and approval gates.

The earlier academic computation took about five months. DeepMind's run took 3.2 days from its first full-scale sieving job to the verified root, reaching about 300,000 CPU cores and 16 GPUs at peak. The authors attribute that calendar-time difference mainly to parallelism.

The CPU saving arose from implementation and execution changes within the existing algorithm. The 391-core-year total excludes about 330 reserved GPU-hours, of which about 100 were busy, and 7.5 core-years of probes and rehearsals. The CPU totals also come from different hardware, so this is not a controlled like-for-like comparison.

The cryptographic setup also matters: a separate program holding the modulus factorization answered roughly 4 billion advance queries. It was withdrawn before the target was drawn. The agents then computed the target's root without further queries.

The measured reproduction did not demonstrate the paper's new algorithm for more restricted signing access at cryptographic size. A separate Fan Factories paper estimates roughly 30-fold lower costs per additional 1024-bit target than the multiple number field sieve, after shared precomputation costing about one general number field sieve factorization. These are leading-order heuristic estimates; no fan factory has been implemented.

The working paper identifies the principal models only as A and B and links no public implementation repository, limiting outside comparisons.

#5132. Hyperscale Data (GPUS) Sells Its Last Bitcoin for AI Data Center, Months After Chasing $100 Million Treasury

Hyperscale Data sold its remaining 211.56 bitcoin for about $16 million by Nov. 8, bringing sales since late July to about 1,113 BTC as it races to energize 10 MW of AI capacity in Michigan in December.

Hyperscale Data has sold the last of its bitcoin, the NYSE American-listed company said Tuesday, unloading about 211.56 BTC for roughly $16 million to pay down debt and fund an AI data center in Michigan.

The sales were completed by Nov. 8 at about $76,000 per coin. Since it first sold part of its reserve in late July, Hyperscale has sold approximately 1,113 bitcoin for about $74.4 million, the company said.

That works out to an average of roughly $66,800 per coin. At today’s price near $74,200, the same 1,113 BTC would be worth about $82.6 million.

The company, which trades under the ticker GPUS, said the money will go toward its Michigan site, where it aims to energize the first 10 megawatts of critical IT capacity in December.

“We believe bringing that capacity online is our quickest path to profitability,” CEO Will Horne said in the release. “Selling our Bitcoin reserves reduces our exposure to Bitcoin price swings and gives us cash to pay down debt and fund the work in Michigan. We believe that’s the best use of this capital for all our stockholders.”

The exit is a sharp reversal from Hyperscale’s plans this summer. In late July, the company reported holding more than 1,106 bitcoin and said it wanted to build a $100 million digital asset treasury and reach full parity between its bitcoin holdings and its market capitalization.

“Every Bitcoin we acquire further strengthens Hyperscale Data’s balance sheet and expands our financial flexibility,” Executive Chairman Milton “Todd” Ault III said at the time. “We intend to continue building our Bitcoin position over time.”

A week later, Hyperscale disclosed its first sale, about 150.5 BTC, leaving it with roughly 958.5 BTC as of Aug. 2, even as its Ault Capital Group subsidiary bought about 15 BTC on the open market. The holdings were split between that unit and Sentinum. Ault said then that the company planned to keep a long-term position while tapping it for short-term flexibility, adding, “We are confident in our ability to use Bitcoin as pristine collateral.”

Tuesday’s release closes that chapter. Hyperscale said it still mines bitcoin at its Montana site and expects any bitcoin it holds on its balance sheet going forward to come “primarily” from its own mining operations.

Hyperscale is the latest public company to give up a bitcoin treasury in favor of data center spending. Keel sold its entire bitcoin treasury for $192 million in the third quarter, and Riot and Hut 8 sold thousands of bitcoin to fund AI buildouts and buybacks.

Larger miners are moving the same way. MARA said Monday it sold 13,597 BTC for about $1.1 billion after Sept. 30 and plans to keep selling to fund AI infrastructure, convertible note puts and share repurchases.

Hyperscale’s structure is more complicated than a pure-play miner’s. Its Sentinum subsidiary runs the data center business, while Ault Capital Group, a hybrid private equity firm and operating company, holds a mix of lending, defense, industrial and hotel businesses. Hyperscale expects to divest Ault Capital Group in 2027 and become a data center owner and operator.

The company said it expects to file its third-quarter 10-Q on or before Nov. 23. Because of a newly proposed exchange offer for its Class A common stock, it is also moving its virtual Investor Day from Nov. 12 to Nov. 23, when management plans to update investors on debt reduction and the December energization target.

Hyperscale did not say how much debt the bitcoin proceeds have retired so far or how much remains outstanding.

#5127. NYSE Taps Avalanche to Settle Its Planned Tokenized Stock Platform

NYSE Taps Avalanche to Settle Its Planned Tokenized Stock Platform

The New York Stock Exchange is turning to Avalanche to power the behind-the-scenes plumbing of its forthcoming tokenized securities platform, one of the clearest signs yet that Wall Street’s oldest institutions are moving core market infrastructure onto public blockchains.

Ava Labs, the company behind Avalanche, said Monday that the blockchain will serve as the “core ledger technology” for the clearing firm behind an NYSE-affiliated digital trading venue.

The platform, which the NYSE’s parent Intercontinental Exchange previously said it was developing, is designed to allow 24/7 trading, clearing and settlement of tokenized securities, subject to regulatory approval. Running on Avalanche, it aims to bring the clearing of tokenized equities onchain at institutional scale.

Tokenization, the practice of issuing traditional assets as blockchain-based tokens, has become one of Wall Street’s buzziest pursuits, but most efforts so far have centered on individual products rather than the market machinery itself.

The NYSE’s move is notable because it puts a blockchain underneath the clearing and settlement layer, the plumbing that finalizes trades, rather than just wrapping a single fund or stock in a token.

Dennis Lee, the NYSE’s head of digital issuance, said the exchange is “picking the right technology for each job,” and that while its planned platform will support equities listed across a range of blockchains, the ledger recording and settling trades needs to be fast, reliable and able to control who participates.

Emin Gün Sirer, Ava Labs’ CEO and founder, framed the deal as proof that blockchains can support not just products but the infrastructure they trade on, citing Avalanche’s “24/7 atomic settlement” and predictable costs.

The announcement adds to a frenetic race to put stocks and their underlying infrastructure onchain.

The NYSE separately tapped Blockchain.com to reach crypto investors with tokenized stocks and ETFs, while ICE and crypto exchange OKX are planning a 24/7 tokenized stock venue under an SEC exemption, and Morgan Stanley has moved to tokenize securities.

That OKX-ICE effort has hit friction, though: Every Magnificent Seven stock, including Apple and Meta, opted out of having its shares tokenized on the venue, with 67 companies in all joining them.

Research shows the appetite for tokenized stocks is real but uneven. An IMF study found tokenized stocks show genuine demand yet remain volatile and illiquid, a reminder that the infrastructure may be arriving faster than the markets to fill it.

#5125. MARA Sells 13,597 Bitcoin for $1.1 Billion, Says More Sales Are Coming

MARA sold about 40% of its bitcoin stack after Sept. 30, used $750 million to repay all its BTC-backed term loans and said it will keep selling to fund AI infrastructure, convertible note puts and buybacks.

MARA Holdings sold 13,597 bitcoin for about $1.1 billion after the third quarter ended and used $750 million of the cash to pay off all of its bitcoin-backed term loans, the miner said Monday in its Q3 shareholder letter.

The coins went for roughly $81,039 each. MARA held 34,012 BTC on Sept. 30, so the sale cut about 40% of the stack in a matter of weeks.

Repaying the loans returned 17,477 bitcoin that had been pledged as collateral, leaving less than 5% of MARA’s holdings loaned or pledged, the company said. Subtracting the sale from the quarter-end figure implies about 20,400 BTC left, before counting coins mined since.

The letter makes clear the selling is not over. “We intend to continue using bitcoin to build cash for purposes such as AI infrastructure opportunities, to satisfy the puts on our convertible notes that become exercisable next year, and potential share repurchases,” MARA wrote.

The board also authorized a buyback of up to $500 million of common stock after quarter-end.

MARA spent years building one of the largest bitcoin stacks among public companies. The shift away from holding came in stages. The company said it began permitting sales of mined bitcoin in 2025 and in 2026 expanded the policy to cover bitcoin already on its balance sheet.

It sold about 26,984 bitcoin for $1.9 billion in the first nine months of the year, including 3,891 BTC in the third quarter at an average of $75,300. It mined 2,247 BTC in the quarter and bought none.

Year to date, MARA has cut total debt by $1.4 billion, or 37%. It ended September with $946.5 million in cash and about $3.8 billion in cash and bitcoin combined, plus 1,408 BTC lent out that earned about $2.5 million in interest during the quarter.

MARA’s post-quarter sale fetched about $6,800 more per coin than bitcoin’s price near $74,200 on Tuesday morning.

The quarter’s headline profit came from the coins, not the mines. Revenue fell 35% to $164.2 million from $252.4 million a year earlier, even as energized hashrate rose 18% to 71.2 EH/s.

Net income rose to $632.1 million, or $1.28 a diluted share, from $123.1 million, helped by an $885.3 million gain on the fair value of digital assets.

Mining itself got slightly more expensive. Purchased energy cost per bitcoin at MARA’s owned sites was $39,674, up from $39,235 a year earlier, while blocks won rose 2% to 644.

“Bitcoin built the foundation. Power created the opportunity,” the letter opens, describing a strategy to “maximize the value of every megawatt” MARA controls.

MARA said it is targeting two data center leases before year-end but warned that “market conditions are fluid and that timing could slip into next year.” It received FERC approval for its Long Ridge natural gas plant purchase, currently authorized to sell 485 MW, and expects to close in the coming weeks. It also secured rights to develop a Matagorda County, Texas site with up to 2 GW of power capacity, and its Exaion unit signed a four-year, $79 million GPU-as-a-service contract with its first U.S. customer.

The move puts MARA in step with peers pulling away from bitcoin. Riot and Hut 8 sold thousands of bitcoin to fund AI projects and buybacks, Keel sold its entire treasury, and Core Scientific plans to exit mining by year-end.

MARA still describes bitcoin mining as its operating foundation, one that keeps sites earning revenue while higher-value infrastructure is built out. With roughly 13,600 fewer coins on the books and a stated plan to keep selling, the miner that once carried one of the largest corporate stacks is now using that stack to pay for its next business.

#5122. Tom Lee’s Bitmine Adds $20M in Ethereum, Seizing on Vitalik’s 'ETH Is Money' Declaration

Tom Lee’s Bitmine Adds $20M in Ethereum, Seizing on Vitalik’s 'ETH Is Money' Declaration

Bitmine Immersion Technologies extended its weekly Ethereum buying streak, adding 9,587 ETH worth roughly $20 million, as chairman Tom Lee pointed to a recent declaration by Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin as validation of the firm’s accumulation strategy.

The NYSE-listed company said Monday its holdings reached 6,070,092 ETH, worth roughly $13.6 billion at a reference price of $2,234 per coin.

That’s 4.97% of Ethereum’s 122.2 million token supply, leaving Bitmine, by its own count, 99% of the way to its goal of owning 5% of the network, a target it calls the “Alchemy of 5%,” reached in just 15 months.

The firm has bought Ethereum every week since launching its treasury strategy on June 30, 2025.

Lee leaned heavily on comments Buterin made at the Devcon conference in Mumbai, where the Ethereum founder said, “I’ve finally made up my mind, ETH is a store of value, ETH is money.” Lee called the declaration “a seismic shift,” arguing it clarifies how ETH will capture value in what he described as a coming “supercycle of tokenization and AI.” (Disclosure: Tom Lee is one of several investors in Dastan, Decrypt’s parent company.)

He contended ETH functions as “pristine and trusted collateral” rather than a cash-flow token, reflecting its position as the layer-1 network favored by financial institutions moving assets onchain.

Buterin elaborated in an X post, laying out why he now sees ETH primarily as a store of value, including his view that fee-burning is weaker than it once seemed and that optimizing for it can conflict with decentralization. Lee framed that reasoning as consistent with Ethereum’s roadmap and its role in the tokenization wave.

Counting cash, other tokens and “moonshot” investments, Bitmine’s total holdings stood at $14.3 billion as of Nov. 8, including 216 Bitcoin, $475 million in cash and marketable securities, a $180 million stake in Beast Industries and a $75 million position in Eightco Holdings, which it bills as a rare public proxy for indirect OpenAI exposure.

Bitmine remains the world’s largest Ethereum treasury and the second-largest crypto treasury overall, trailing only Michael Saylor’s Strategy, which the release said holds about 849,327 BTC. Bitmine has 5,227,037 ETH, roughly 86% of its holdings, staked through its MAVAN platform, with projected annualized staking revenue of about $359 million.

The firm also recently argued the muted market reaction to the record Binance hack showed crypto’s growing resilience.

#5119. Trump Media (DJT) Pledges 73% of Its Bitcoin to an Options Program as $1 Billion Note Deadline Nears

Trump Media's Q3 10-Q shows 11,385 of its roughly 15,649 bitcoin pledged to an options program whose counterparty can reuse the coins, with nearly all the rest backing $1 billion of notes holders can put back Nov. 30.

Trump Media & Technology Group has pledged about 73% of its bitcoin to an options program in which the counterparty can reuse the coins, the company disclosed in its third-quarter 10-Q filed Monday, three weeks before holders of its $1 billion in convertible notes can demand cash.

The Truth Social parent held approximately 15,649 BTC on Sept. 30, Chief Financial Officer Phillip Juhan said on Monday’s earnings call, along with 7 million shares of BlackRock’s IBIT. Of those coins, 11,385.20 were pledged to what the company calls its bitcoin yield management program.

The filing says that program requires Trump Media to post bitcoin as collateral “that the counterparty can rehypothecate at their sole discretion.” The pledged coins carried a fair value of $951.4 million at quarter-end. The 10-Q does not name the counterparty.

Another 4,260.73 BTC, worth $356.1 million on Sept. 30, sits as collateral for the convertible notes and cannot be withdrawn or distributed until the indenture’s conditions are met.

Together, the two buckets account for about 15,646 BTC, nearly all of the stack Juhan described.

Trump Media sells and buys covered calls and puts on bitcoin, settled in bitcoin, to “generate yield on these assets and increase our principal balance of bitcoin,” the filing says. Premiums arrive in bitcoin and are “immediately rehypothecated to our digital asset manager to reinvest.”

At quarter-end it had written calls referencing 4,838.40 BTC at strikes from $68,000 to $92,000 and puts on 1,500 BTC at $75,000 to $80,000, all expiring in October.

A risk factor spells out the trade-off. The company says its yield counterparties “may not be rated” by credit agencies, that it is limited in its ability to sell or use deployed bitcoin while the arrangements are open, and that where they are unsecured “we may be unable to recover deployed bitcoin in a counterparty insolvency.”

Juhan said Trump Media bought 4,359 bitcoin during the quarter with proceeds from a partial sale of its IBIT position, part of a shift toward “third-party institutional” management of its treasury.

The bitcoin rally in the third quarter turned Trump Media profitable on paper. Net income was $409.7 million, driven by a $378.1 million gain on digital assets as bitcoin climbed to about $84,000 on Sept. 30 from about $59,000 on June 30. Adjusted EBITDA was still a loss of $12.3 million, and the company lost $234.2 million over the first nine months.

Prices have since moved against the stack. With bitcoin near $74,200 Tuesday morning, the 15,649 coins are worth about $1.16 billion, roughly $145 million less than at quarter-end.

The bigger test is the notes. Holders of the $1 billion in 0% senior secured convertibles, due May 2028, can require Trump Media to buy them back at full principal for cash on Nov. 30. General Counsel Scott Glabe said notices have gone out and holders have until near the end of the month to respond, so the company cannot yet say how much it will owe.

Interim CEO Kevin McGurn said the plan is “a mix of cash and credit” rather than new equity. “We want to preserve as much of our Bitcoin as possible to continue our yielding strategy and allow that asset to recover,” he said.

The 10-Q says the company may enter a new credit facility to refinance some or all of the notes, but adds that “there can be no assurance” it can do so on acceptable terms. Juhan put gross financial assets at $2.3 billion, including $182 million in cash, $211 million in short-term investments and $1.7 billion in bitcoin and bitcoin-related assets.

Trump Media is not the only treasury company under pressure. Strategy, the largest corporate holder, slipped below its average cost on Monday. Trump Media also faces more political scrutiny after Democrats won Congress, with party leaders vowing to target Trump family crypto ventures and incoming Senate Banking Chair Elizabeth Warren preparing her own oversight push.

Shareholders vote Dec. 14 on the company’s planned merger with fusion energy firm TAE Technologies, which management expects to close by year-end.
